'''Cynthia J. Burrows''' is an American chemist, currently a distinguished professor in the department of chemistry at the [[University of Utah]], where she is also the Thatcher Presidential Endowed Chair of Biological Chemistry. Burrows was the Senior Editor of the ''[[Journal of Organic Chemistry]]'' (2001-2013) and became Editor-in-Chief of ''[[Accounts of Chemical Research]]'' in 2014.<ref name=":0" /><sup>,</sup><ref>{{Cite web|title=Cynthia Burrows, PhD - Faculty Details - U of U School of Medicine - {{!}} University of Utah|url=http://medicine.utah.edu/faculty/mddetail.php?facultyID=u0031358|access-date=2017-06-02|website=medicine.utah.edu|language=en}}</ref><sup>,</sup><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Cynthia Burrows|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/cynthia-j-burrows-ebcden/|access-date=2017-06-02|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>

==Education and training==
Burrows acquired a B.A. degree in chemistry at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]] (1975). There she worked on [[Stern-Volmer experiment|Stern-Volmer plots]] in [[Stanley J. Cristol]]'s laboratory during her senior year. She continued to study [[physical organic chemistry]] at [[Cornell University]], where she received a Ph.D. degree in chemistry in 1982 working in [[Barry Carpenter]]'s laboratory. Her Ph.D. thesis work focused on cyano-substituted allyl vinyl ethers. Burrows then conducted a short post-doctoral research stint with [[Jean-Marie Lehn]] in [[Strasbourg]], [[France]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burrows|first1=Cynthia J.|last2=Carpenter|first2=Barry K.|date=1981-11-01|title=Substituent effects on the aliphatic Claisen rearrangement. 1. Synthesis and rearrangement of cyano-substituted allyl vinyl ethers|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=103|issue=23|pages=6983–6984|doi=10.1021/ja00413a045|bibcode=1981JAChS.103.6983B |issn=0002-7863}}</ref><ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Cynthia J. Burrows |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/burrows-cynthia-j|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="transcript">{{cite book|first=Hilary L.|last=Domush|title=Cynthia J. ==Career and research==
[[File:Types of DNA Damage.jpg|thumb|DNA can be damaged by the disruption of base pairs.]]The [https://chem.utah.edu/directory/burrows/research-group/index.php Burrows laboratory] is interested in nucleic acid chemistry, DNA sequencing technology, and DNA damage. Her research team (consisting of organic, biological, analytical and inorganic chemists) focuses on chemical processes that result in the formation of mutations, which could lead to diseases (such as cancer). Her work includes studying site-specifically modified DNA and RNA strands and [[Crosslinking of DNA|DNA-protein cross linking]].  Burrows and her group are widely known for expanding the studies on nanopore technology by developing a method for detecting DNA damage using a nanopore.<ref name=":0" /><sup>,</sup><ref name=":2" />

One of the objectives of the Burrows Laboratory is to apply nanopore technology to identify, quantify, and analyze DNA damage brought on by oxidative stresses. Burrows focuses on the damage found in human telomeric sequences, crucial chromosomal regions that provide protection from degradation and are subject to problems during [[DNA replication]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=An|first1=Na|last2=Fleming|first2=Aaron M.|last3=Burrows|first3=Cynthia J.|date=2016-02-19|title=Human Telomere G-Quadruplexes with Five Repeats Accommodate 8-Oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine by Looping out the DNA Damage|journal=ACS Chemical Biology|volume=11|issue=2|pages=500–507|doi=10.1021/acschembio.5b00844|issn=1554-8929|pmc=4828913|pmid=26686913}}</ref> Additionally, Burrows’ research in altering nucleic acid composition can provide valuable information in genetic diseases as well as manipulating the function of DNA and RNA in cells.

===Nanopore detection of DNA damage===
[[File:Guanine Oxidative Damage.jpg|thumb|The Burrows research lab focuses on detecting guanine oxidation reaction as shown.]][[File:Nanopore_detection_diagram_of_DNA_damage.jpg|thumb|DNA strand passes through the a-hemolysin nanopore and allows researchers to detect single base damaged site. The goal of this nanopore detection system is to locate damaged sites and understand how a damage at a specific site leads to disease.]]
Nanopore technology is significant in analysis of biological macromolecules such as DNA and RNA because it can detect minute sample quantities and bypasses the need for [[Polymerase chain reaction|PCR]] amplification. PCR amplification and other DNA sequencing methods cannot detect DNA damage alone because their basis relies on the four classical unmodified bases: [[cytosine]], [[adenine]], [[guanine]], and [[thymine]]. One of the most common and prevalent causes of DNA damage is oxidation of guanine residues to 8-oxoguanine brought on through oxidative stresses. 8-oxoguanine causes mismatch pairing with adenine as opposed to cytosine, which can ultimately cause point mutations during DNA replication.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cheng|first1=K. C.|last2=Cahill|first2=D. S.|last3=Kasai|first3=H.|last4=Nishimura|first4=S.|last5=Loeb|first5=L. A.|date=1992-01-05|title=8-Hydroxyguanine, an abundant form of oxidative DNA damage, causes G----T and A----C substitutions|journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry|volume=267|issue=1|pages=166–172|doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)48474-8|issn=0021-9258|pmid=1730583|doi-access=free}}</ref> In the context of DNA-protein cross linking, 8-oxoguanine is susceptible to forming adducts with amino acids containing reactive groups such as the phenol moiety of tyrosine or terminal amine of lysine.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xu|first1=Xiaoyun|last2=Fleming|first2=Aaron M.|last3=Muller|first3=James G.|last4=Burrows|first4=Cynthia J.|date=2008-08-06|title=Formation of tricyclic [4.3.3.0] adducts between 8-oxoguanosine and tyrosine under conditions of oxidative DNA-protein cross-linking|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=130|issue=31|pages=10080–10081|doi=10.1021/ja803896d|issn=1520-5126|pmid=18611013}}</ref><sup>,</sup><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xu|first1=Xiaoyun|last2=Muller|first2=James G.|last3=Ye|first3=Yu|last4=Burrows|first4=Cynthia J.|date=2008-01-16|title=DNA-protein cross-links between guanine and lysine depend on the mechanism of oxidation for formation of C5 vs C8 guanosine adducts|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=130|issue=2|pages=703–709|doi=10.1021/ja077102a|issn=1520-5126|pmid=18081286}}</ref> Detection and quantification of 8-oxoguanine content in telomeric sequences is important because content increases with stress since telomeres escape cellular DNA repair mechanisms.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=An|first1=Na|last2=Fleming|first2=Aaron M.|last3=White|first3=Henry S.|last4=Burrows|first4=Cynthia J.|date=2015|title=Nanopore detection of 8-oxoguanine in the human telomere repeat sequence|journal=ACS Nano|volume=9|issue=4|pages=4296–4307|doi=10.1021/acsnano.5b00722|issn=1936-086X|pmc=4790916|pmid=25768204}}</ref> Burrows helped to discover specific DNA glycosylases that preferentially repaired oxidative damages at telomeric sites.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zhou|first1=Jia|last2=Liu|first2=Minmin|last3=Fleming|first3=Aaron M.|last4=Burrows|first4=Cynthia J.|last5=Wallace|first5=Susan S.|date=2013-09-20|title=Neil3 and NEIL1 DNA glycosylases remove oxidative damages from quadruplex DNA and exhibit preferences for lesions in the telomeric sequence context|journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry|volume=288|issue=38|pages=27263–27272|doi=10.1074/jbc.M113.479055|issn=1083-351X|pmc=3779722|pmid=23926102|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Nanopore technology relies on passing a constant electric current through a nanoscale hole immersed in an electrolytic solution. Molecules that pass through or disrupt the current by blocking the pore will generate a detectable signal when measuring current versus time. Nanopores can range from solid-state constructs to small proteins. To examine the extent of damage in G-quadruplexes of telomeres, Burrows used a protein α-hemolysin, which contains a nanoscale tube core and is embedded in the cell membrane.<ref name=":1" /> Damaged bases are oxidatively marked with a crown ether to amplify the current signal as well as to reduce the mitigating effects of 8-oxoguanine on the native fold.<ref name=":1" /> As the DNA strand passes through, the marked damaged base produces a characteristic signal as it disrupts the applied current.
